clinical_scope.population: Adults and young people aged 16 years or older unless otherwise specified by local protocol
excluded_populations: pediatric specialty pathways unless explicitly validated
clinical_scope.intended_use: High-risk candidate retrieval and guideline-based verification for suspected Bowel Perforation.
clinical_scope.important_boundary: This graph supports clinical reasoning and missed-diagnosis risk reduction; it is not an autonomous diagnostic system.

relationship_to_other_graphs.boundary_note: This graph targets suspected bowel/hollow viscus perforation. Etiology-specific pathways such as perforated peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, appendicitis, ischemic bowel, trauma, or iatrogenic perforation should be loaded when identified.

basic_info.working_definition: Bowel perforation is a full-thickness breach of the gastrointestinal wall allowing gas, enteric contents, or infection to enter the peritoneal or adjacent spaces.
why_high_risk_for_missed_diagnosis: Early symptoms may be nonspecific, especially in older, immunosuppressed, or steroid-treated patients.
Free air may be absent depending on location, sealed perforation, or imaging timing.
Perforation can mimic gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, biliary disease, renal colic, obstruction, mesenteric ischemia, or sepsis of unclear source.
Delayed source control can lead to peritonitis, sepsis, shock, and death.
basic_info.time_sensitivity: Suspected perforated viscus with peritonitis, sepsis, free air, or hemodynamic instability requires urgent surgical evaluation, broad-spectrum antimicrobial pathway, resuscitation, and source-control assessment.

graph_nodes.name: Change in bowel habits or obstruction symptoms
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast when appropriate
Upright chest radiograph or abdominal radiograph for free air when CT delayed/unavailable
Lipase and liver tests for mimics
Portal venous gas or pneumatosis in ischemic context
Broad-spectrum antimicrobial pathway for suspected complicated intra-abdominal infection
Fluid resuscitation for sepsis or hypoperfusion
Nil per os and supportive care per local protocol
Critical care escalation if shock or organ dysfunction
Do not delay surgery/source control in unstable peritonitis

activation_logic.minimum_activation: Acute severe abdominal pain, peritonitis, sepsis with abdominal source, free air/extraluminal gas, or high-risk perforation context.

strong_activation_patterns.reason: Peritonitis pattern suggesting perforation or surgical abdomen.
Imaging evidence strongly supports perforated viscus until proven otherwise.
Possible intra-abdominal source requiring source control.

case_features: abdominal pain without peritonitis, sepsis, risk factors, or imaging

symptom_to_candidate_retrieval.scoring_warning: Weights are for retrieval and explanation only. They are not calibrated probabilities and must not be used as a diagnostic score.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Are acute abdomen, peritonitis, sepsis, or perforation risk factors present?
guideline_verification_pathway.negative_result: Lower priority but continue if high-risk context.
guideline_verification_pathway.if_missing: Abdominal exam/vitals missing; cannot safely down-rank.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Are hypotension, tachycardia, fever/hypothermia, elevated lactate, organ dysfunction, or shock present?
guideline_verification_pathway.positive_result: Escalate resuscitation, sepsis, and surgical source-control urgency.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Is CT abdomen/pelvis or other imaging available to evaluate free air, perforation site, abscess, obstruction, or ischemia?
guideline_verification_pathway.negative_result: If imaging negative but peritonitis persists, surgical assessment remains important.
guideline_verification_pathway.if_missing: Perforation cannot be confirmed/excluded without appropriate imaging and clinical judgment.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Are labs and cultures available to evaluate infection, organ dysfunction, and operative risk?
guideline_verification_pathway.positive_result: Use data for severity and antimicrobial/source control planning.
guideline_verification_pathway.negative_result: Normal labs do not exclude early perforation.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Is there a source requiring surgery, drainage, repair, resection, or device/foreign body management?
guideline_verification_pathway.negative_result: Nonoperative management may be considered only in selected stable contained cases by specialists.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Is complicated intra-abdominal infection likely requiring broad-spectrum antimicrobial pathway?
guideline_verification_pathway.negative_result: Avoid unnecessary broad treatment if perforation/infection unlikely.

guideline_verification_pathway.check: Can the likely cause/location be identified: peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, appendicitis, ischemia, obstruction, IBD, malignancy, trauma, or iatrogenic?
Could mesenteric ischemia, pancreatitis, obstruction, AAA rupture, renal colic, DKA, or gastroenteritis explain the presentation?
guideline_verification_pathway.positive_result: Report competing diagnoses; some require equally urgent action.
guideline_verification_pathway.negative_result: Perforation remains likely if peritonitis/free air/source evidence present.

distinguishing_features: Pain out of proportion, atrial fibrillation/vascular risk, elevated lactate; can progress to perforation.
Distension, vomiting, obstipation; perforation risk if strangulated/closed-loop.
Epigastric pain radiating to back, high lipase; can cause SIRS without perforation.
RUQ pain, jaundice, fever, abnormal LFTs.
RLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis; perforated appendicitis is a source subtype.
Back/abdominal pain, shock, pulsatile mass; catastrophic vascular mimic.
Flank pain, urinary symptoms; sepsis possible in infected obstruction.

final_assessment.safety_statement: Clinical decision support only; urgent clinician assessment is required when a high-risk condition is suspected.

evidence_sources.title: 2017 WSES guidelines for management of intra-abdominal infections
key_points: Management of complicated intra-abdominal infections involves source control and antibiotic therapy.
Used here for bowel perforation-related peritonitis, urgent surgical assessment, antimicrobial therapy, and source control principles.

evidence_sources.title: IDSA guideline update on complicated intra-abdominal infections: risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation
key_points: Updated recommendations span risk assessment, diagnostic imaging, and microbiological evaluation for complicated intra-abdominal infections.
Used here for imaging, microbiology, and risk-assessment elements related to suspected bowel perforation and intra-abdominal sepsis.

evidence_sources.title: Bowel Perforation
key_points: Risk history includes obstruction, malignancy, foreign body, abdominal trauma, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and chemotherapy.
Used for broad risk-factor and presentation nodes, supplemented by surgical/infectious disease guidelines.

must_not: Do not make an autonomous definitive diagnosis.
Do not use a single symptom, sign, laboratory result, score, or imaging clue as a standalone rule-in or rule-out criterion.
Do not provide patient-facing reassurance when critical red-flag data are missing.
Do not ignore competing high-risk differential diagnoses.
Do not replace local emergency, specialty, or hospital protocols.
Do not generate medication orders; recommend clinician-led pathway activation instead.
Do not exclude perforation because free air is absent on plain radiograph.
Do not delay surgical consultation in unstable peritonitis while waiting for complete labs.
Do not label severe abdominal pain with peritonitis as gastroenteritis without imaging/surgical assessment.
must_do: Use this graph for candidate retrieval, missed-diagnosis risk reduction, and guideline-based verification.
Separate supporting evidence, evidence against, and missing critical information.
State whether verification is complete, partial, impossible from available data, or contradicted.
Include differential diagnoses that can mimic the condition.
Trace guideline-dependent claims to evidence IDs.
Mark output as clinical decision support requiring qualified clinician review.
Always assess peritonitis, sepsis/shock, imaging status, and source-control need.
Always list medication/procedure risk factors such as NSAIDs, steroids, chemo, endoscopy, or trauma.
